title: Charlie Parker
summary: Wilson knew Parker only slightly from record dates and a WNEW session; Hinton recalls him as a serious talker who later fell into drugs.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Did you know Bird much? Charlie?

Not too close. I've made several record dates with him and some jam sessions and jazz concerts. I remember once when I was down at WNEW, he came out a few times as guest with the house band, and they'd have some jazz sessions there.
I didn't have too many close talks with him, you know, like with Coleman or Benny Carter. Because Charlie
from out of Kansas City, you know, he came with Jay McShann and Gus Johnson and Gene Raney Randall, they came about 1940 or so to New York.
So I didn't know him as well as these fellows in New York, because I always had lived in New York after I came from Chicago in '33. I was completely out of touch with the Kansas City group.
Did you ever hear Charlie say anything seriously like that, like Coleman, his views on life?
His views, yes, he was a very serious person like that, too. Charlie used to come by, when I was with Cab Calloway, he'd come by the theater and just sit back-stage and talk very seriously.

No, it was more lyrical about the injustices and social things in the world. And then again, I would see him later, when he got involved in drugs and the whole scene, and he would just be out of it. But when he was together, he was a very serious talker. And of course I did -- not too many records, but I did a lot of jam sessions with him, always a joy.
But you know something, both you and I, we've read the books about the people that he come up with and all that, and you've really got to laugh at these books because they're
so different from the way we really saw him.
